stories.title: Investment Team Inks $125M Construction Loan for Miami Design District Office/Retail Project
stories.excerpt: Miami Design District Associates and Raycliff Capital broke ground on an office/retail project in the Miami Design District. The S. Florida Business Journal reports that the group began work on the project soon after securing a $125 million construction loan. Credit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank, acting on behalf of a group of lenders, granted the mortgage. The eight-story building will feature 92,000 square feet of office space and 22,500 square feet of ground-floor retail. The neighboring Museum Garage will provide the parking spaces for the project. Norway-based Snøhetta is designing the project It’s work includes the Bibliotheca Alexandrina in Egypt, the Norwegian National Opera and Ballet, and the National September 11 Memorial Museum Pavilion in New York. Kast Construction is serving as the general contractor. The post Investment Team Inks $125M Construction Loan for Miami Design District Office/Retail Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Miami Design District: $125M construction loan from Credit Agricole for 92k SF office + 22.5k SF retail
8-story mixed-use project breaking ground with 22.5k SF ground-floor retail component
Office/retail development signals continued capital availability for Miami mixed-use projects
stories.summary: Miami Design District Associates and Raycliff Capital secured a $125 million construction loan from Credit Agricole to begin an eight-story mixed-use project featuring 92,000 square feet of office and 22,500 square feet of ground-floor retail in the Miami Design District. The project is designed by Snøhetta and will rely on the adjacent Museum Garage for parking. The loan and groundbreaking signal renewed lender confidence in Miami's office and mixed-use development pipeline.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact to multifamily. The office/retail focus and financing availability signal capital is flowing to mixed-use in Miami, but this project displaces office and retail demand rather than creating residential demand signals. Monitor whether retail-focused mixed-use projects in Miami compress multifamily absorption by reducing the project pipeline diversity developers compete for.

stories.title: Investors Are Gaining More Confidence in Office: Survey
stories.excerpt: Investment appetite for office transactions is showing signs of a revival in 2026. Preference from commercial real estate investors for office transactions reached 11 percent in the second quarter. That compares to just 4 percent in early 2025 who listed the office sector as the one with the most opportunities, according to SitusAMC’s latest ValTrends quarterly research report shared exclusively with Commercial Observer ahead of its scheduled release later this week. While office sentiment in the survey was lower than the 16 percent registered in the first quarter, overall trends within the property sector are on the upswing following years of investor confidence in the asset class hovering in the low single digits, said Peter Muoio, head of SitusAMC Insights. Muoio said more clarity on valuations is driving the renewed interest. Increased pressure on some distressed debt may also be a contributing factor behind the numbers, Muoio added. “We’ve been seeing over the past year or year and a half the office investment conditions are improving,” Muoio said. “There is renewed interest.” Part of the increased bullishness toward office investments, according to Muoio, stems from “growing optimism” with the financial feasibility of executing office conversions. The report showed that office cap rates tightened by 10 basis points (bps) in the second quarter, but remained 80 bps above their long-term average. The increasing enthusiasm for office investments in the ValTrends report is part of a more evenly split preference for property types that has been developing over the past year, according to Muoio. Multifamily remained the top-ranked asset class in the second quarter, but optimism cooled in the survey from 60 percent to 36 percent compared to the previous quarter. Muoio said the drop was likely attributed to oversupply issues, particularly in the Sun Belt, taking longer to resolve than initially anticipated. bullets: SitusAMC survey: office investor preference rose to 11% in Q2 2026 vs. 4% in early 2025
Valuation clarity and distressed-debt pressure driving renewed office investment appetite
Office sentiment below Q1 peak of 16% but well above prior low single-digit baseline
stories.summary: According to SitusAMC's ValTrends research, investor preference for office transactions reached 11 percent in Q2 2026, up from just 4 percent in early 2025, signaling a nascent revival in office investment. Clearer valuations and pressure on distressed office debt are cited as drivers. Despite being below Q1's 16 percent level, the trend represents a significant turnaround from years of investor disinterest in the office sector.
stories.impact: Office revival may redirect institutional capital away from multifamily value-add and development. Developers competing for mixed-use sites or Class A repositioning deals could face stiffer bidding from office-focused investors, tightening land and acquisition costs across major metros. Monitor whether cap-rate compression in office limits equity availability for multifamily development.

stories.title: Bank Capital’s Riskiest Bonds Are Pricing Like the Safest
stories.excerpt: Executive Summary Additional Tier 1, or AT1, bank bonds are trading at near-historic tight spreads despite their complex, loss-absorbing structures. With the ICE CoCo Index offering roughly 206 basis points over benchmark rates, well below its 385-basis-point historical median, investors may not be adequately compensated for coupon-cancellation, extension, and regulatory risks. As banks increasingly issue securities with 10-year rather than five-year initial call periods, AT1s are becoming more duration-sensitive and less of a straightforward credit investment. Yield Demand Drives Spreads Tighter AT1 bonds, commonly called CoCos, were created after the 2008 financial crisis to provide banks with loss-absorbing capital before taxpayer support would be needed. They sit above common equity but below most other bank debt in the capital structure. Their coupons are generally discretionary, perpetual, and issuers can write down principal or convert the instruments into equity if specified capital triggers are breached. The fundamental outlook for many global banks remains sound. Common Equity Tier 1 ratios are generally well above regulatory minimums, while earnings and loan-loss reserves have supported confidence in issuers’ ability to service their debt. That strength, combined with demand for yield, has helped drive AT1 valuations higher. But the ICE CoCo Index’s options-adjusted spread has compressed to roughly 206 basis points over benchmark rates, compared with a historical median of approximately 385 basis points. The narrowing spread leaves little room for deteriorating risk sentiment, volatility, a discretionary coupon cancellation or a reassessment of bank funding costs. The Credit Suisse Reminder The asset class carries a powerful reminder of its asymmetric risk. In March 2023, regulators wrote down approximately $17 billion of Credit Suisse AT1 bonds to zero as part of the bank’s emergency takeover by UBS. The loss represented roughly 10% of the global AT1 ind
bullets: AT1 bank bonds trading at 206 bps vs. 385 bps historical median; investors undercompensated for risk
Banks extending call periods from 5 to 10 years, increasing duration risk on perpetual coupon instruments
Strong bank fundamentals (CET1 ratios above minimums, earnings solid) masking structural and regulatory tail risks
stories.summary: Additional Tier 1 (AT1) bank bonds are trading at historically tight spreads (206 basis points vs. 385 bps median) despite their loss-absorbing structures and coupon-cancellation risks. Banks are increasingly issuing longer-duration (10-year call) AT1s rather than shorter 5-year initial calls, raising extension and regulatory risk. While bank fundamentals remain sound, investors may be underpricing the embedded risks in these complex securities.
stories.impact: If AT1 spreads blow out on a credit or regulatory shock, bank capital constraints could tighten construction loan availability and raise multifamily development financing costs. Monitor banking system stability; a flight to safety in bank capital could cascade to reduced mortgage lending and higher SOFR/construction loan spreads affecting pro forma returns across development pipelines.

stories.title: Development Team Pursuing S. Nashville Hotel, Apartments
stories.excerpt: The proposal, which is weaving its way through Nashville’s approval process, includes a hotel, apartments and an ice rink in the middle. The Nashville Business Journal reports the entities tied to Darshan Patel and Richard Epperson will go before the Metro Planning Department for approval on Sept. 24. The project, slated to rise at 4311 and 4319 Sidco Drive, will include two apartment buildings with ground-level retail and a 16-story hotel. (rendering courtesy Nashville Post) In the center of it all, a large plaza is planned, with renderings indicating that it will offer an outdoor ice rink. The properties currently house a La Quinta Inn and the Bedroom Nashville Event Venue, which would need to be demolished to make way for the new development. A Cracker Barrel and a Waffle House are located on either side of the project site. They’ll stay put. The post Development Team Pursuing S. Nashville Hotel, Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: South Nashville development: 2 apartment buildings, 16-story hotel, ground-level retail + ice rink plaza; Sidco Drive site
Developers Darshan Patel and Richard Epperson seeking approval Sept. 24 from Metro Planning Department
Mixed-use project targets demolition of La Quinta Inn and Bedroom Nashville Event Venue; flanked by Cracker Barrel and Waffle House
stories.summary: A mixed-use development team led by Darshan Patel and Richard Epperson is pursuing approval for a South Nashville project at 4311–4319 Sidco Drive that includes two apartment buildings with ground-floor retail, a 16-story hotel, and a central plaza with an outdoor ice rink. The project requires demolition of a La Quinta Inn and Bedroom Nashville Event Venue. Metro Planning Department approval is scheduled for September 24.
stories.impact: Nashville multifamily supply continues to grow with mixed-use delivery pipelines. This Sidco Drive project adds apartment units to a competitive South Nashville submarket where rent growth has moderated; monitor absorption pace and per-unit rents post-delivery to assess whether added supply pressures existing portfolio performance or achieves strong lease-up velocity. The hotel and experiential plaza suggest the developer is hedging multifamily-only risk, a rational approach in a maturing market.

stories.title: JLL Arranges $34M Sale of Bridge Point Tacoma 210
stories.excerpt: JLL arranged the $33.9 million sale of Bridge Point Tacoma 210, a 205,413-square-foot distribution facility located at 10917 34th Ave. E in Tacoma, Washington. JLL represented the seller, Kurv Industrial, in the transaction. Completed in 2024, Bridge Point Tacoma 210 represents one of the newest industrial deliveries in Pierce County and features institutional-grade specifications designed for modern distribution operations. The JLL Capital Markets team was led by Managing Director James Ellis and Director Rachel Jones. The single-story facility offers 36-foot clear heights, 50 dock-high doors, two grade-level doors and 130-foot truck courts on 13.82 acres. The property includes 24 trailer stalls situated on nearly one acre of excess yard space and provides 130 auto parking spaces. The distribution is located five miles from Interstate 5, and nine miles from the Port of Tacoma. “Bridge Point Tacoma 210 attracted strong institutional interest due to its new construction quality and strategic location at the confluence of Tacoma’s premier submarkets,” said Ellis. The post JLL Arranges $34M Sale of Bridge Point Tacoma 210 appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Kurv Industrial sold Bridge Point Tacoma 210: 205k SF industrial facility, $33.9M, completed 2024
36-foot clear heights, 50 dock-high doors, 13.82 acres near Interstate 5 and Port of Tacoma
New industrial construction attracted institutional buyers; recent completion and premium specs supported valuation
stories.summary: JLL arranged the $33.9 million sale of Bridge Point Tacoma 210, a 205,413-square-foot industrial distribution facility completed in 2024. The single-story property features 36-foot clear heights, 50 dock doors, and 13.82 acres, located five miles from Interstate 5 and nine miles from the Port of Tacoma. Strong institutional interest reflects demand for newly built, modern distribution space in Pierce County.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact. Tacoma industrial market remains active and well-capitalized, but this sale signals robust logistics/distribution demand tied to Port of Tacoma activity. Multifamily developers should monitor whether port-driven employment growth and warehouse job creation sustains Tacoma rental demand; if logistics employment stalls, multifamily absorption could weaken despite apparent industrial vigor.

stories.title: Investor Team Picks Up Walmart-Anchored Raleigh Retail Center
stories.excerpt: Corebridge Real Estate Investors and a fund from Armstrong Capital Development are teaming up to acquire and develop retail assets in select high-growth markets across the United States. The venture completed its inaugural acquisition with the purchase of Townridge Shopping Center, a 273,105-square-foot retail center in Raleigh. JLL Capital Markets secured the $36 million sale and $26.5 million acquisition financing of Townridge Shopping Center, which is anchored by Walmart. The center was 96 percent leased at the time of sale. Zeisler-Morgan Properties was the seller. JLL Capital Market’s Investment Sales and Advisory team, led by Tom Kolarczyk, Michael Nieder and Brian Page, represented the seller. Travis Anderson and Ward Smith secured the financing. Corebridge Real Estate Investors is the real estate equity investment management division of Corebridge Financial. CREI has an $8 billion portfolio of real estate assets under management, consisting of approximately 35 million square feet. The post Investor Team Picks Up Walmart-Anchored Raleigh Retail Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Corebridge and Armstrong Capital acquired Townridge Shopping Center, Raleigh: 273k SF Walmart-anchored retail, $36M sale price
Center was 96% leased at sale; $26.5M acquisition financing secured by JLL
Corebridge has $8B AUM and ~35M SF portfolio; inaugural acquisition for new retail venture
stories.summary: Corebridge Real Estate Investors and Armstrong Capital Development partnered to acquire Townridge Shopping Center in Raleigh, a 273,105-square-foot Walmart-anchored retail center, for $36 million. The center was 96 percent leased at closing. JLL arranged $26.5 million in acquisition financing. This is the inaugural deal for the retail-focused venture targeting high-growth markets.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. Raleigh retail fundamentals appear stable (96% occupancy, strong anchor), but this transaction reflects capital flowing to retail stabilization rather than growth development. Monitor whether Corebridge's retail focus signals institutional preference for stabilized, lower-risk asset classes, which could reduce equity availability for higher-risk multifamily development in Raleigh and other Sunbelt markets.

stories.title: Mexican Restaurant Santo Taco Subleases Former West Village Dig Inn Space
stories.excerpt: Santo Taco is subleasing space formerly occupied by Dig Inn in Manhattan’s West Village, Commercial Observer has learned. The Mexican food concept launched by Santiago Perez in 2025 will take over the 2,800-square-foot, street-level and below-grade space at the Steven Fuchs-owned 232 Bleecker Street at the corner of Bleecker and Carmine streets, according to ManagRE. The sublease runs until 2041. ManagRE did not disclose the asking rent in the off-market deal, but the average asking rent in nearby retail corridors in the Meatpacking District was $252 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE. Navin Bhutani of ManagRE was the sole broker in the deal, and Meerkat Development is managing the buildout of the space. Dig Inn did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Fuchs, who owns a number of properties in the West Village, could not be reached for comment. Santo Taco already has two locations at 114 Kenmare Street and 94 University Place with the new location opening next month. Perez was the CEO of Mexico City-based firm Casamata Hospitality for 10 years, managing concepts like Enrique Olvera’s Pujol as well as Cosme in the Flatiron District and Damian in Los Angeles. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Santo Taco subleases 2.8k SF former Dig Inn space, 232 Bleecker Street (West Village, Manhattan), through 2041
Meatpacking District nearby retail averaging $252/SF asking rent in Q2 2026
Dig Inn closure signals tenant turnover and sublease availability in prime Manhattan retail corridors
stories.summary: Santo Taco, a Mexican restaurant concept launched in 2025, subleased a 2,800-square-foot street-level and below-grade space formerly occupied by Dig Inn at 232 Bleecker Street in Manhattan's West Village. The long-term sublease runs through 2041. Nearby Meatpacking District retail averaged $252 per square foot in asking rent in Q2 2026. The deal signals ongoing turnover and sublease opportunities in prime Manhattan retail.
stories.impact: Minimal multifamily impact. Dig Inn's retreat from West Village reflects consumer preferences and restaurant operating challenges, not macro demand signals. However, sustained retail turnover and sublease leakage in prime Manhattan neighborhoods can depress ground-floor retail absorption in new multifamily developments, pressuring mixed-use project returns and reducing development feasibility in high-cost urban cores.

stories.title: Goodland Pickleball Takes 30K SF for New Indoor Clubs in Brooklyn, Queens
stories.excerpt: Indoor pickleball club operator Goodland Pickleball has secured two new club locations in New York City, Commercial Observer has learned. The long-term leases span a total of 30,100 square feet within Class A buildings in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, and Rego Park, Queens. Goodland, which secured its first indoor New York City club in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood in 2024, reports more than 11,000 members across the city. Goodland’s Williamsburg lease, located at Rabsky Group’s 105 North 13th Street, is slated to become its new flagship location. Spanning 14,600 square feet, the club will feature four courts across two floors with 20-foot ceilings, as well as a private fifth-floor court, an outdoor terrace and a sushi bar. The Williamsburg site attracted competition from multiple pickleball operators, Hemant Chavan, founder and CEO of Goodland Pickleball, told CO. Chavan called the site “a needle in a haystack,” estimating that fewer than two dozen indoor spaces suited to pickleball’s lofty space needs exist in the city. Goodland declined to provide the asking rent, but asking retail rents along Bedford Avenue’s nearby North Eighth and North 12th streets corridor averaged $245 per square foot in the latter half of 2025, according to the Real Estate Board of New York (the most recent data available). A rendering of Goodland Pickleball’s planned facility in Rego Park, Queens. RENDERING: Courtesy Goodland Pickleball Goodland represented itself in both lease deals, the second of which landed Goodland 15,500 square feet at RB Realty Capital’s 98-22 Queens Boulevard in Rego Park. The location will accommodate six courts, including a badminton court. Recent asking rents for Queens retail spaces averaged $42.47 per square foot, according to data from CommercialCafe. Both of Goodland’s new sites belong to Class A buildings. bullets: Goodland Pickleball secured 30.1k SF across two Class A locations: 14.6k SF Williamsburg flagship, 15.5k SF Rego Park
Williamsburg site (105 North 13th St, Rabsky Group) features 4 courts, private 5th-floor court, outdoor terrace, sushi bar
Operator reports 11k+ members across NYC; high ceiling requirements limit available subleasing options
stories.summary: Goodland Pickleball signed two long-term leases totaling 30,100 square feet in Class A buildings in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, and Rego Park, Queens. The Williamsburg flagship at Rabsky Group's 105 North 13th Street spans 14,600 square feet with four courts, a private fifth-floor court, outdoor terrace, and sushi bar. Goodland now operates three NYC clubs with 11,000+ members and cited extreme scarcity of spaces meeting pickleball's 20-foot ceiling requirements.
stories.impact: Pickleball expansion signals strong amenity demand in Brooklyn and Queens residential markets. Mixed-use multifamily developers should consider pickleball facilities as tenant draw and rent-premium justification in Class A Brooklyn (Williamsburg, Greenpoint) and Queens (Rego Park) projects. Limited indoor pickleball supply (< 2 dozen suitable spaces in NYC per operator) suggests pre-leasing opportunities for new multifamily communities if space configuration allows.

stories.title: National Resources Sells New York-Area Mixed-Asset Portfolio for $450M
stories.excerpt: The wait was well worth it. A more than year-long process that began last summer when National Resources CEO Lynne Ward contacted Marty Berger, co-founder of Saber-Hightower, about selling a mixture of commercial real estate assets across the New York City region as part of an estate sale produced a winning result. A joint venture between Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower and Waterfall Asset Management acquired four National Resources properties encompassing more than 4million square feet in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, for $450 million, Commercial Observer has learned. The acquisition, which is anchored by iPark 84, a 270-acre business park in East Fishkill, N.Y., took longer than usual to close given the amount of acreage involving three states, according to Jared Toothman, executive vice president and New York City metro market leader at Lincoln. Toothman said Berger invited him to his golf club to discuss the deal and later added Waterfall to the partnership after pitching the opportunity to investors. “We shook hands on it over a card table at a golf club and then we were off to the races,” Berger told CO. “We took a very long time to really get our hands around a portfolio to be able to extract all the pieces.” The iPark 84 property 50 miles north of Manhattan consists of a 1.8 million-square-foot campus originally developed for IBM’s flagship semiconductor manufacturing plant. It has a diverse tenant mix that includes IBM, Samsung subsidiary eMagin and agricultural company Cal-Maine, and can accommodate 1.5 million square feet of additional development The sale also features a 29-acre, mixed-use center at 761 Main Street in Norwalk, Conn., anchored by a Northwell Health medical outpatient complex, The roughly 400,000 square-foot property includes the corporate headquarters of bicycle company Cannondale, a 70,000-square-foot gym and space for approved multifamily development. The transaction also consists of Edgewater Harbor, in Edgewater, N.J
bullets: National Resources estate sale: Lincoln Property, Saber-Hightower, Waterfall AM acquired $450M multi-asset portfolio
Portfolio: 4M+ SF across NY, NJ, CT; anchored by iPark 84 (270-acre business park, East Fishkill, N.Y.)
Year-long process; multi-state complexity and acreage extended closing timeline; institutional joint-venture structure
stories.summary: A joint venture of Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower, and Waterfall Asset Management acquired a $450 million portfolio from National Resources comprising four properties totaling over 4 million square feet across New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut. The anchor asset is iPark 84, a 270-acre business park in East Fishkill, New York. The transaction took over a year to close due to multi-state complexity and large acreage.
stories.impact: iPark 84 is a large office/industrial park; its acquisition by institutional capital signals continued flight-to-quality in suburban Hudson Valley markets. Multifamily developers in Westchester and Hudson Valley should monitor whether this large estate conversion and institutional repositioning creates spillover development activity (road improvements, infrastructure) or diverts capital from residential development. Estate sales of this magnitude can unlock land but also fragment ownership and may trigger extended holding periods before residential development becomes feasible.

stories.title: REITs Report Strong Q2 Results Even as Interest Rates Weigh on Investor Sentiment
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) performed strongly in the second quarter of 2026 — led by impressive showings in the hospitality, industrial and office sectors — but the industry as a whole remains handicapped by high interest rates and a lack of investor confidence. These are the conclusions from a new report by Hoya Capital, a private investment advisory and research company that specializes in the REIT space. Hoya Capital accumulated data from over 200 U.S. REITs and homebuilders which reported second-quarter earnings results in recent weeks, finding that 83 percent of publicly traded REITs raised full-year funds from operation (FFO) guidance — a proxy for cash flow — while just 4 percent lowered their outlooks. “Overall, REIT earnings results were surprisingly strong and delivered one of the cleanest reporting periods in recent memory, with unusually broad guidance raises, improving property-level fundamentals, and relatively few outright disappointments,” wrote Hoya Capital. The firm found that in the second quarter of 2026, national office leasing rose 16 percent year-over-year to 62.4 million square feet, buoyed by strong earnings by office giants SL Green Realty and BXP. At the same time, retail occupancy has nearly returned to pre-pandemic levels, and the industrial sector rode the data center development wave. “Higher-for-longer interest rates have been in place for a while now and REITs are finding ways to operate in a very volatile environment, whether that’s raising billions in capital or engaging in mergers and acquisitions or portfolio sales,” said David Auerbach, chief investment officer at Hoya Capital. Despite the good news, high interest rates are truly beginning to damper investor sentiment toward REITs as a whole, especially over the last month. bullets: 83% of REITs raised full-year FFO guidance in Q2 2026; only 4% lowered outlooks; strong earnings reported
Office leasing rose 16% YoY national; hospitality and industrial sectors led REIT performance
High interest rates and weak investor confidence persist despite strong Q2 property-level fundamentals
stories.summary: Hoya Capital's analysis of 200+ U.S. REITs and homebuilders found that 83 percent raised full-year FFO guidance in Q2 2026, with just 4 percent lowering outlooks. Hospitality, industrial, and office sectors led REIT performance, while office leasing rose 16 percent nationally. Despite strong property-level fundamentals and earnings, the sector remains pressured by elevated interest rates and weak investor confidence.
stories.impact: Multifamily REITs likely contributed to strong earnings but face capital-markets headwinds. High interest rates continue to constrain multifamily development starts and refinancing yields; elevated cap rates and slowing rent growth in many markets offset operational strength. Developers should expect continued cost-of-capital pressure through 2026 unless Fed cuts rates materially. REIT strength suggests equity capital is available for acquisitions, but debt financing for new development remains constrained, favoring builds-to-suit, JV structures, and debt partnering over traditional leverage.
